title: Just Enjoying Things
author: Foster
summary: A pastor and writer reflects on why he has deliberately refused to turn his lifelong love of comic books and boxing into monetized content, using it as a case study in the corrosive effect of audience capture on anything a person genuinely loves. He traces how creators who start out sharing a hobby out of love often drift into producing whatever converts followers into paying subscribers, a process that eventually kills the original passion, and connects this directly to his own experience gaining an unwanted public platform after a piece he wrote on manhood unexpectedly went viral. Rather than lean into that platform, he explicitly refuses to write for audience approval, arguing that maintaining a genuinely independent, even prophetic, voice as a pastor requires 'a general disregard for what people want you to say, do, or write,' and citing Henry Ford's apocryphal line about customers wanting a faster horse rather than a car. He closes by describing comics as 'modern mythology' rather than financial investments, and frames his refusal to monetize his hobbies, and his effort to teach his children to enjoy things without turning them into content, as a form of freedom that a heavily monetized influencer life would cost him.
points: The essay's core diagnostic is a pattern he has observed in other creators: sharing a hobby out of love, gaining an audience, then shifting to producing whatever converts followers into paying subscribers, a process that kills the original passion.

He connects his own experience of unwanted platform growth (after 'It's Good to Be a Man' went viral) directly to a decision to withhold his comics and boxing interests from being converted into content.

His claim that maintaining a 'prophetic voice' as a pastor requires 'a general disregard for what people want you to say, do, or write' explicitly frames audience-responsiveness as being in tension with independent moral or spiritual authority.
He reframes comic books as 'modern mythology' rather than financial assets, rejecting the investment-collector framing common among fellow enthusiasts he encountered online.
He extends the lesson to parenting, describing active efforts to teach his children to enjoy things 'just for themselves' rather than as material for public sharing or validation.
quotes: My reason is that not everything needs to be content. Not everything needs to be monetized. Some things should just be enjoyed for what they are.
Before long, what they were sharing out of love became a slog that actually caused them to lose interest in the thing they had loved so much. I don't want that.
To be very clear, I don't write for you. It will be a cold day in hell before I cater to anyone to hang on to them as a subscriber, follower, or even church member.

If you want to maintain a prophetic voice, meaning a voice that speaks with clarity on the issues of the day, there is a degree of independence you have to maintain as a writer and pastor. And that means having a general disregard for what people want you to say, do, or write.
I was thinking about how they don't understand comics. They're not investments for money. They're modern mythology. They're stories to captivate, inspire, comfort, and challenge.
I am free. I am so free. And I won't put a price on that freedom because I know part of the cost is spoiling the things you love.
